title: Standard library HTTP server instead of a web framework
context: The repo was empty, with no dependency tooling or framework chosen.
options: FastAPI or Flask: request validation, docs and production servers for free, but adds dependencies and a packaging setup
Standard library http.server: runs with a bare Python install, but routing is by hand and it is not a hardened production server
why: The service has three routes, so a framework buys little here, and zero dependencies means it runs and tests with nothing to install. The storage layer is separate from the HTTP layer, so swapping in a framework later only touches server.py.

title: Random 7-character base62 codes rather than encoded sequential ids
context: Each link needs a short unique code.
options: Base62 of an auto-increment id: shortest possible codes and no collisions, but links are enumerable and reveal how many exist
Random base62 from the secrets module: not guessable, needs a retry when a code collides
Hash of the URL: deterministic, but forces deduplication and still needs collision handling
choice: Random base62 from secrets, 7 characters, retry on collision
why: 7 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes, so collisions are rare and the primary key catches them. Random codes keep other people's links from being walked by counting upwards.

title: SQLite file with one shared connection behind a lock
context: Links must survive restarts, and the server handles requests on multiple threads.
options: In-memory dict: simplest, but links are lost on restart
SQLite, one shared connection plus a lock: persistent, no dependency, writes are serialised
SQLite, one connection per thread: more concurrency, but more lifecycle code and in-memory test databases stop being shared
Postgres or Redis: scales out, needs an external service
choice: SQLite, one shared connection plus a lock
why: Persistence with no setup, and every operation is a single-row statement so the lock is held very briefly. It is a single-process design, so several server processes would need a different store.

title: 302 redirects, not 301
context: The redirect status decides whether browsers cache the hop.
options: 301 permanent: browsers cache it, so fewer requests, but repeat visits skip the server and are never counted
302 found: every visit reaches the server, so click counts are right
why: The service counts clicks, and a cached 301 would silently undercount them.

title: Only http and https targets are accepted
context: A shortener redirects visitors to whatever was stored, so the stored URL is a security boundary.
options: Accept any URL: flexible, but allows javascript: and data: targets and header injection through control characters
Allow only http/https with a host, no whitespace or control characters, ASCII host: stricter, rejects some unusual links
choice: Allow only http/https with strict validation
why: The URL is written into a Location header, so anything else is an open door for script URLs and response splitting. Non-ASCII paths are percent-encoded; non-ASCII hostnames are rejected and must be given as punycode.

title: Shortening the same URL twice gives two separate links
context: A repeated URL could either reuse the existing code or get a new one.
options: Deduplicate: fewer rows, but everyone who shortens that URL shares one click counter, and it conflicts with custom aliases
New code each time: more rows, each link has its own counter
why: Click counts stay meaningful per link and no lookup-by-URL index is needed.

title: Short URLs are built from the Host header unless --base-url is set
context: The API returns a full short URL, so the server has to know its own public address.
options: Require a configured base URL: always correct, but one more thing to set before the first run
Use the request's Host header, with an optional --base-url override: works out of the box, but the header is client-controlled and is wrong behind a proxy or TLS terminator
why: It keeps local use to one command. A client can only influence the short URL in its own response, but any real deployment should set --base-url, which also fixes the http:// scheme.

title: Custom aliases and click counts are included in the first version
context: The request was for a URL shortener, with no feature list.
options: Shorten and redirect only: the smallest thing that fits the request
Also custom aliases, click counts and a web form: what people usually expect from a shortener, at the cost of more surface to review
choice: Include aliases, click counts and a web form
why: Each is a few lines on top of the core, and they shaped other choices (302 redirects, no deduplication), so it was cheaper to settle them now. They are easy to remove if unwanted.
